NTSB:20260112202283.s: The pilot of a Stinson 108-3 sustained minor injuries when the aircraft pancaked on a private airstrip in Colorado after encountering sinking air and an engine sputter during a sharp throttle increase on short final. Although the engine monitor showed no malfunction, insufficient data prevented confirming a power loss before the hard landing caused substantial damage.

NTSB:20260112202284.n: The pilot was conducting a landing in the tailwheel-equipped airplane when during landing roll the airplane began to swerve right. The pilot was unable to regain directional control using a left rudder input. The airplane departed the right edge of the runway and impacted a split rail fence before it came to rest. The fuselage, right wing, right-wing struts, and vertical stabilizer were substantially damaged during the runway excursion. The pilot did not report any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation of the airplane. However, after the accident he located a removable plastic cup holder under the left rudder pedal for the rear seat position. The pilot reported that he flew the airplane from the front seat position. The pilot purchased the airplane 7 days before the accident. After the accident, the pilot contacted the previous owner of the airplane who confirmed that the removable cup holder had been left in the airplane. Based on the available information, it is likely the removable cup holder became wedged under the left rudder pedal for the rear seat position, which restricted the movement of the interconnected (front/rear) left rudder pedals. Without left rudder pedal input, the pilot only had left brake to correct for the right swerve during landing roll.
NTSB:20260112202284.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane lost directional control during landing roll after a removable cup holder wedged under the left rudder pedal. This restriction prevented rudder input, causing the aircraft to swerve right, depart the runway, and impact a fence with substantial damage.

NTSB:20260112202285.n: The pilot reported that upon runway contact, the airplane began to pull to the right and not slowing down like it normally would. The pilot attempted to keep the aircraft on the runway centerline by applying full left rudder. Subsequently, the pilot lost directional control as the airplane spun perpendicular to the runway. The nose landing gear collapsed, and the airplane came to rest on the runway. The pilot reported that he was not sure if the green gear down indicator lights were illuminated prior to landing. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the lower skins, stringers, and box beams on the fuselage. After the airplane was recovered from the runway, the pilot noticed the landing gear circuit breaker was tripped. Upon resetting the circuit breaker, the landing gear lowered and locked in the down position. Postaccident examination did not reveal why the circuit breaker had tripped.
NTSB:20260112202285.s: The pilot lost directional control during landing when the aircraft pulled right and spun, collapsing the nose gear. The pilot attributed the incident to a tripped landing gear circuit breaker that prevented gear extension, though the cause of the trip remained undetermined.

NTSB:20260113202289.n: On January 7, 2026, at about 0809 mountain standard time, a Beech K35, N6010E, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Prescott, Arizona. The pilot and flight instructor were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The pilot receiving instruction reported that upon arriving at the Prescott Regional/Ernest A Love Field Airport (PRC), Prescott, Arizona, they conducted an ILS approach to runway 21L. After they completed a touch and go landing and takeoff, they noted a positive rate of climb and retracted the landing gear. At about 50 ft agl, they heard a loud "bang" and observed the airplane's propellor completely stop. The flight instructor then pushed the control yoke forward to maintain airspeed. Unable to maintain altitude the pilot initiated a gear up forced landing to the remaining runway. During the landing flare the airplane landed hard, which resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage and empennage. The airplane was recovered for further examination.
NTSB:20260113202289.s: During a Part 91 instructional flight in a Beech K35, the propeller stopped at 50 feet AGL after gear retraction following a touch-and-go. The crew executed a gear-up forced landing, resulting in substantial fuselage and empennage damage from a hard landing, though both occupants were uninjured.

NTSB:20260113202290.n: Shortly after takeoff, during the initial climb, the pilot stated that he perceived that the airplane's engine noise was louder than normal. After ensuring that the pilot and passenger side windows were closed and locked, he decided that he would decrease the engine throttle slightly to diagnose the sound. When the pilot reached for the throttle, he inadvertently grabbed the mixture control, and after pulling it back, the engine lost power completely. The pilot attempted to restart the engine twice, but both attempts were unsuccessful. As the airplane was approaching a tree line, and only at an altitude of about 300 ft above the ground, the pilot decided to turn back to a field that was near the end of the runway. The pilot subsequently landed the airplane off-airport, and during the landing roll the nose landing gear encountered a rut. The airplane subsequently nosed over, resulting in substantial damage to the airplane's rudder and wings. The pilot reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260113202290.s: During initial climb, a pilot inadvertently pulled the mixture control instead of the throttle, causing total engine power loss. The pilot executed an off-airport landing at 300 feet, where the nose gear hit a rut, nosing over the aircraft and damaging the rudder and wings.

NTSB:20260113202292.n: The pilot of the balloon reported that during the flight, the wind pattern changed, and the balloon had traveled toward a congested area. The pilot attempted to land in a clearing, however, decided to abort the landing with the application of the burners to initiate a climb. Subsequently, the pilot realized that the balloon would not clear a set of power lines ahead of their position and pulled out the top of the balloon to expedite a descent. The balloon impacted the power lines and support pole, which resulted in substantial damage to multiple basket suspension cables. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the balloon that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260113202292.s: The balloon pilot encountered changing winds and aborted a landing attempt, then intentionally deflated the envelope to descend but struck power lines and a support pole. This impact caused substantial damage to multiple basket suspension cables, with no pre-accident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260113202294.n: On January 13, 2026, about 0624 mountain standard time, a Fairchild SA227-AC airplane, N370AE, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Prescott Municipal Airport (PRC), Prescott, Arizona. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 positioning flight. According to the pilot, he began the takeoff roll on Runway 3R for a scheduled flight to Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (KPHX), Phoenix, Arizona. The pilot reported that during a normal takeoff roll, when the aircraft was accelerating through about 50 kts, the airplane began to veer left and subsequently departed the left side of the runway, entering the runway safety area. The airplane then crossed a taxiway before the pilot maneuvered it back onto the runway and brought it to a stop. During the runway excursion, the airplane collided with runway edge lights and a taxiway sign, resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage. The airplane and engine were recovered and will be examined.
NTSB:20260113202294.s: The pilot of a Fairchild SA227-AC operating a Part 135 positioning flight reported that the aircraft veered left at 50 knots during takeoff roll on Runway 3R at Prescott Municipal Airport. The excursion caused the airplane to strike runway edge lights and a taxiway sign, resulting in substantial fuselage damage, though the pilot was uninjured.

NTSB:20260114202297.n: On January 13, 2026, about 1530 eastern standard time, a Cessna 177B, N34959, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ocoee, Tennessee. The pilot received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, the airplane had been undergoing maintenance for the past 11 months following a propeller strike. The repairs and the annual inspection were completed the day before the accident flight. After refueling the fuel tanks and performing a preflight inspection, with no anomalies observed, he departed from Lovell Field Airport (CHA), Chattanooga, Tennessee, and proceeded east. About 20 minutes after departure, and at an altitude of 4,500 ft mean sea level (msl), the engine rpm increased to 3,000 rpm, which is 300 rpm above the engine's maximum operating rpm, followed by an engine vibration. The pilot declared an emergency to air traffic control but determined he would be unable to reach the nearest airport and initiated a forced landing in a field. During the landing rollout, the airplane continued into a wooded area and impacted trees. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed it had sustained substantial damage to the wings, the fuselage, and the horizontal stabilator. A coating consistent with engine oil was observed on the left side of the engine and fuselage. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260114202297.s: The pilot of a Cessna 177B experienced an engine overspeed to 3,000 rpm and vibration at 4,500 ft msl shortly after departing Chattanooga. This forced a landing in a wooded area, resulting in substantial damage to the aircraft and minor injuries to the pilot.

NTSB:20260114202298.n: On January 13, 2026 about 1220 mountain standard time, a Cessna 750, N772XJ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Mountain Village, Colorado. The pilots and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 as an on-demand air taxi flight. The pilots reported that during the airplane's descent into Telluride Regional Airport (TEX), they encountered turbulent conditions with a strong northwesterly wind resulting in airspeed fluctuations between 5 and 10 kts. They aligned the airplane with runway 9 and the wind was shifting between north and northeast. The touchdown was smooth and on centerline. Spoilers were deployed and forward pressure was applied on the control column to keep the nosewheel in contact with the runway. Shortly after touchdown, the airplane encountered a strong gust of wind from the left (north). The airplane veered to the right and the nose came up momentarily. Both pilots applied firm pressure on the control column and the nosewheel contacted the runway again. Thrust reversers were deployed along with an input of left rudder. The airplane veered sharply to the left. Both pilots applied right rudder, maximum braking and reverse thrust to regain directional control. The airplane continued to the left and exited the side of the runway. The left main gear sideloaded, and the right main gear collapsed. The pilots stated that the airplane did not respond normally when they corrected for the right drift. The fuselage was substantially damaged. The airplane was retained for further examination. Reported wind at TEX at 1215 was 020° at 4 kts.
NTSB:20260114202298.s: Pilots of a Cessna 750 operating a Part 135 flight exited the runway at Telluride Regional Airport during landing due to strong gusts causing directional control loss. The aircraft sustained substantial damage when the right main gear collapsed after veering off the side of the runway, though no occupants were injured.

NTSB:20260114202300.n: The pilot of the airplane reported that during the takeoff roll from a private dirt airstrip, the engine suddenly lost power. As he scanned the instrument panel and engine controls, he observed the fuel selector valve lever in the OFF position. He switched the fuel selector valve to BOTH and noticed that the propeller had stopped turning. Subsequently, the airplane exited the departure end of the runway, impacted a ditch, and nosed over. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left lift strut, vertical stabilizer, and rudder. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. Additionally, the pilot reported that he should have used the checklist. (Fuel was in the "OFF" position).
NTSB:20260114202300.s: The pilot reported that during takeoff from a private dirt airstrip, the engine lost power because the fuel selector valve was in the OFF position. After switching the valve to BOTH, the propeller had stopped, causing the airplane to exit the runway, impact a ditch, nose over, and sustain substantial damage.

NTSB:20260115202302.n: The pilot reported that during the approach to land at an off-airport location, the helicopter entered an uncommanded right rotation. He attributed the loss of control to unfavorable winds and described the event as consistent with a loss of tail rotor effectiveness. He was unable to regain control, and the helicopter continued to descend in a spiraling right spin before it impacted the ground and rolled over. As a result, the helicopter sustained substantial damage to the fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260115202302.s: During approach to an off-airport landing, a helicopter pilot experienced an uncommanded right rotation attributed to unfavorable winds and loss of tail rotor effectiveness. Unable to regain control, the aircraft spiraled into the ground, rolled over, and sustained substantial fuselage damage with no pre-accident mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260115202303.n: In preparation for the personal flight, the pilot started the airplane to warm the engine. He then set the airplane's parking brake and exited the airplane to load baggage while the engine was operating at idle. He asked the passenger, who was not a pilot, to board the airplane while the baggage was being loaded and to pull the mixture control if anything should happen. The pilot then went into the fixed base operator to get his debit card and to use the bathroom. Within two minutes, he heard the engine sound increase, and the airplane taxi into an unoccupied vehicle that was parked about 75 yards away. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the outboard section of right wing. The pilot reported there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. The pilot stated that the accident could have been prevented by never placing an unattended non-pilot passenger in parked operating airplane and would be scheduling remedial pilot training with a flight instructor.
NTSB:20260115202303.s: The pilot left a non-pilot passenger in an idling aircraft with the parking brake set to load baggage and retrieve a debit card. The passenger failed to secure the engine, causing the airplane to taxi into a parked vehicle and sustain substantial right wing damage.

NTSB:20260115202304.n: The flight instructor was going to demonstrate to the pilot receiving instruction, a short-field takeoff, with a simulated loss of engine power, as required per the flight school lesson plan. The flight instructor reported that he configured the airplane for the takeoff. Once the airplane had climbed to about 100 ft agl, he reduced the engine power to idle and began the descent back to the runway. The flight instructor noticed that the flight controls "seemed heavy" and the airplane was "descending fast." The airplane landed hard on the runway and came to rest upright. The airplane taxied to the ramp without further incident, the airplane was shut down, and both occupants departed. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage. Postaccident examination of the airplane found the elevator trim was set to the full nose down position for the takeoff. The operator reported there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airframe or the engine that would have precluded normal operation. The operator further reported that the accident could have been prevented if the flight instructor had adhered to the published maneuver procedure and profile, for the maneuver that was being demonstrated. The airplane's before takeoff checklist includes a step to configure the elevator trim for the takeoff. The FAA Aviation Instructor's Handbook FAA-8083-9B discusses checklists and states in part: Checklists are essential flight deck resources for verifying that the aircraft instruments and systems are checked, set, and operating properly, as well as ensuring that the proper procedures are performed if there is a system malfunction or inflight emergency.
NTSB:20260115202304.s: A flight instructor and student pilot experienced a hard landing during a simulated short-field takeoff in a training aircraft. The accident occurred because the elevator trim was set to full nose-down, causing heavy controls and a rapid descent, resulting in substantial fuselage damage.

NTSB:20260117202309.n: The pilot maneuvered the airplane onto the final approach leg of the traffic pattern; he reduced the power to slow the airplane and encountered a significant downdraft or windshear. The airplane impacted the ground about 150 feet short of the runway threshold. The nose and left main landing gear collapsed, and the left wing contacted a snow berm which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and lower fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260117202309.s: The pilot encountered significant downdraft or windshear while reducing power on final approach, causing the aircraft to impact the ground 150 feet short of the runway. The nose and left main gear collapsed, and the left wing struck a snow berm, resulting in substantial damage with no reported mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260117202310.n: Air Transport International (ATI) cargo flight 4340 experienced a hard landing at San Bernadino International Airport (SBD), San Bernadino, California. The unscheduled domestic cargo flight was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 from Spokane International Airport (GEG), Spokane, Washington. The airplane sustained substantial damage and there were no injuries. A postaccident examination of the airplane performed by the operator revealed damage to the crown of the upper fuselage. The fuselage skin was buckled and fractured, as shown in figure 1, with damage to the underlying stringers, lap and butt joints. Figure 1. Fuselage damage on top and right side. (Source: ATI) The flight crew noted no anomalies with the airplane before or during flight. The first officer was the pilot flying. They performed a comprehensive approach briefing for the ILS to runway 6. They checked the automated terminal information system (ATIS) which indicated no concerning weather, with “excellent” VFR conditions and light winds. The airplane intercepted the localizer about 12 miles out, and they both described the approach as stable. The first officer disconnected the autopilot between 250 and 200 ft above the ground as planned. As he heard the automated radio altitude callouts for 50 ft and 40ft, he began to reduce the decent rate, and at 10 ft, he retarded the throttles and prepared for touch down. He recalled the touchdown being normal, and then recognized the nose tended to pitch up. He relaxed the control column and applied forward pressure to prevent further pitch up. “At that moment, the controls moved forward abruptly and forcefully”, which caused him to momentarily lose his grip on the controls. The nosewheel then forcefully contacted the runway. Afterwards, the airplane went back to a steady condition, and he applied left rudder to maintain centerline. At 60 knots, the captain called “my controls” and the first officer transferred the controls to him. The remainder of the rollout and taxi were uneventful. The captain recalled that the landing flare was initiated at the appropriate time, though (at some time) he noticed “what appeared to be an over-rotation causing the plane to balloon.” Concerned about the “high pitch attitude and trend” [and the potential for a tail strike], he stuck his hand out to block the yoke from coming back further. The airplane then “de-rotated rapidly, landing with a jarring impact.” A review of the flight data and cockpit voice recorder readouts revealed that the airplane had initially touched down (air/ground indication of “ground” and sound similar to wheels contacting runway) at an airspeed of about 124 knots, flaps 25°, with a pitch attitude of about 5° nose up, and a control column position of about +12° (positive values are aft of neutral). About 1-2 seconds later, the air ground indication momentarily changed to “air” for a single sample (recorded at 1 second intervals) and then back to “ground” where it remained. Between the two “ground” indications, the control column position reduced to about +6°, and the pitch attitude reduced to about 3°. Just after the second “ground” indication, the control column position increased to about +20° and then immediately reversed and decreased to about -20° (negative values are forward of neutral). The decrease occurred over about 1.5 seconds, and during that time the CVR recorded an utterance from the first officer. Further, during this aft-then-forward control column sequence, the airspeed initially decreased from about 119 to 113 knots, and the pitch attitude increased from about 3° to about 6°, before it decreased to about 0°. This decrease was the derotation to nose landing gear touchdown. As the pitch attitude reached 0°, a large spike in vertical acceleration was recorded (upwards to about 1.6 Gs, then reversed to about 0.1 Gs), consistent with nose landing gear touchdown. While the first officer recalled that the controls moved abruptly forward while he was at the same time already moving it forward, the captain recalled putting his hand up to prevent further movement of the control column aft. The investigation was unable to resolve this discrepancy definitively. However, they both recalled that the derotation occurred just after their respective actions (the blocking of aft movement by the captain, and the loss of grip on the yoke of the first officer). That interaction almost certainly occurred during the +20° to -20° control column sequence, because that sequence ended with the derotation. It may have happened just prior to the first officer’s utterance captured by the CVR. See figure 2. Figure 2. Chart of FDR and CVR data during landing. The captain’s concern about a possible trail strike was likely due to the airplane’s pitch attitude which increased after touchdown and had ultimately reached about 6° nose up. Geometrically, the tail should strike ground at a pitch attitude of about 8° nose up with the main landing gear compressed (see NTSB accident investigation DCA25LA085). The airplane manufacturer’s flight crew training manual advises that pilots should not allow the pitch attitude to increase, or to hold the nose wheel off the runway after landing, which could lead to a tail strike. However, there was no verbal communication between the crew recorded on the CVR at the time of the captain’s intervention, or the first officer’s loss of grip on the yoke. According to the crew’s statements, as well as conversations captured by the CVR after landing (between the captain and first officer, as well as of the captain while on a telephone call), the crew did not realize at the time what exactly had occurred. The first officer didn’t realize that the captain had restricted the aft column motion, and the captain, who was looking at the runway at the time, didn’t see that the first officer’s hands had slipped off the yoke. They discovered this during their after-landing conversations, and concluded that for a period of time, apparently neither one of them were on the controls. The review of the recorded data could not definitively confirm when, or for how long the pilots had their hands off the control yoke. However, it is likely that it began near or after the time that the control column reached its peak value of about 20° aft (because the captain was trying to limit its aft travel) and likely continued through the nose down control column trend at least until the time the pitch attitude reached 0° and the large vertical acceleration was recorded. The manufacturer’s flight crew training manual also advises not to make large nose-down control column movements, to avoid structural damage. Derotation is the lowering of the aircraft’s nose gear to the runway following touchdown on the main gear during landing. In a review of National Transportation Safety Board investigations and assisted international investigations, eight similar derotation accidents involving Boeing 757/767 aircraft were found. Those investigations were: January 16, 1992 - Asiana Airlines in Cheu Island, South Korea October 27, 1992 – American Airlines flight 957 in São Paulo, Brazil December 31, 1993 – LOT flight 002 in Warsaw, Poland July 31, 1997 – Federal Express in Newark, New Jersey May 22, 2002 – Monarch Airlines in Gibraltar April 20, 2009 – Royal Air Maroc flight 200 in New York, New York August 18, 2019 – Delta Air Lines 414 in Ponta Delgada, Portugal July 29, 2023 – United Airlines 702 in Houston, Texas. These accidents occurred when the pilots applied large nose-down control column deflections after main landing gear touchdown, which resulted in large nose-down pitch rates and high vertical velocities at the nose gear. It was this combination of vertical velocity and pitch rate that resulted in compression loads that exceeded the design loads of the forward fuselage crown structure. In 1994, the NTSB made recommendations to the Federal Aviation Administration 1) calling for changes to Boeing 757/767 operating manuals, suggesting they include specific derotation techniques and guidance and 2) modification to initial and recurring Boeing 757/767 training programs to include discussion of derotation accidents. These recommendations were closed in August 1995 as acceptable (NTSB Recommendation Nos. A-94-118 and A-94-119).
NTSB:20260117202310.s: Air Transport International flight 4340 sustained substantial fuselage damage during a hard landing at San Bernardino after the crew lost control of the yoke during derotation. The nose gear impacted the runway with excessive force following a rapid, large nose-down control column movement, causing structural failure without injuries.

NTSB:20260118202312.n: On January 18, 2026, about 1640 central standard time, a Piper PA28-140 airplane, N6711J, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Holly Springs, Mississippi. The flight instructor and student pilot were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. According to the airport manager, the airplane had departed Holly Springs-Marshall County Airport (M41), Holly Springs, Mississippi, after doing several touch and go landings. There was no ADS-B data available for the accident flight. The airplane impacted terrain in a wooded area about 693 ft east of the departure end of runway 18 at M41. The first identified impact point was a pine tree about 185 ft south of the main wreckage. The airplane struck numerous pine trees along the impact path. Five branches were located at the site varying from .75 to 2 in diameter with clean cut marks and black paint transfer consistent with the airplane’s propeller. No ground impact marks were found at the accident site. A post-impact fire consumed a large portion of the airframe. The flight instruments and flight controls were thermally damaged or destroyed. The manual flap selector was thermally damaged and was found in the full flap (40 degree) position. The fuel selector valve was selected to the right fuel tank position and functioned normally when tested with low-pressure air. Flight control continuity was confirmed for the flight controls. The stabilator trim cables were continuous from the empennage to the forward cabin location. The stabilator trim actuator control rod was extended 1.6 in on the top side of the actuator, which was consistent with a partial nose up trim position. The airplane was equipped with a Lycoming O-320-E3D reciprocating engine. The engine remained attached to the engine mount. The propeller assembly was partially embedded in soft dirt. Engine control cable continuity was confirmed from the firewall forward to both the mixture and throttle arms of the engine’s carburetor. The mixture was found halfway between lean and rich while the throttle arm was found at a partial power setting. The engine primer control was found within the wreckage in the forward and locked position. The spark plugs were removed from their respective cylinders. The spark plugs had normal wear patterns, and the coloration was consistent with normal engine operation. The lower plugs on cylinder Nos. 1 and 2 were oil soaked consistent with the oil drained from each cylinder upon removal. The lower spark plug for cylinder No. 3 was found impact fractured below the ignition harness nut. Examination of each cylinder was completed with a borescope with no anomalies found. Thumb suction and compression was confirmed on all cylinders by rotating the propeller in the direction of engine rotation. With all rocker box covers removed, all rocker arms moved freely and through their full range of motion with no anomalies found. The oil lines to the oil cooler were found attached. The oil filter was found attached to the accessory section and safety wired but thermally damaged. The filter was removed, cut open, and inspected. The filter element had burned, but no metallic particles were noted between the remains of the filter pleats. The oil suction screen plug was found tight and secured to the oil sump with safety wire. Once removed, the screen was found free and clear of any debris. The oil filler neck was consumed by fire with only the metal dipstick remaining within the engine case. Oil was present in the oil sump, but total quantity was not determined. Both magnetos were present, secure, and exhibited varying degrees of thermal damage to their aluminum housing. The magnetos were removed and an attempt to rotate them by hand was made. During the attempt, friction was present and both magnetos would bind during rotation. The left-hand magneto was disassembled, and thermal damage was noted internally. The right-hand magneto suffered a higher degree of thermal damage to its aluminum housing and was not disassembled. The engine driven fuel pump was found attached to the rear accessory section of the engine and exhibited thermal damage. All fuel lines were found attached, but the aluminum housing showed signs of melting and deformation. During disassembly of the engine driven fuel pump, the gaskets and diaphragms were found thermally damaged. The fuel pump activation rod was found present within the accessory case and moved freely with rotation of the engine’s crankshaft. The airplane was equipped with a Power Flow Systems Exhaust. The exhaust system was cut free from the engine at each cylinder and checked for blockage. The exhaust system was found free of any blockages or anomalies. All intake pipes were removed and found free and clear of blockage or debris. The carburetor remained attached to the lower side of the engine. The airbox and air duct hoses were found impact or thermally separated. The carburetor was removed from the engine and examined. The float bowl was removed from the carburetor, and no fuel or fluid was found in the bowl. No sediment was present and the brass floats were free of damage or deformation. The needle and seat were present. The seat was free and clear of any damage but showed discoloration consistent with thermal damage. The needle tip was deformed consistent with exposure to the post impact fire. The propeller assembly was found partially embedded in the ground. Both blades remained attached to the propeller hub and the propeller was largely intact. The propellor exhibited slight thermal discoloration to one blade on the cambered side. No observable bending or deformation was noted to either blade. Slight chordwise scratches and smears were noted and consistent with cut pine branches found at the accident site. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260118202312.s: A flight instructor and student pilot were fatally injured when their Piper PA28-140 crashed into trees shortly after departing Holly Springs-Marshall County Airport for an instructional flight. The investigation found no mechanical anomalies, with the accident occurring during climb-out with flaps set to 40 degrees and partial nose-up trim.

NTSB:20260119202313.n: On January 18, 2026, about 1510 mountain standard time, a Bell 206L-1, N138DD, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Kamas, Utah. The pilot and three passengers received minor injuries. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot of the 206L-1, he and another pilot planned to fly their respective helicopters to a mountain lodge for lunch. The other pilot was operating a Robinson R66 helicopter with two passengers onboard. Preliminary ADS-B data retrieved from a commercially available third-party source showed the 206L-1 departing from Skypark Airport (BTF), Bountiful, Utah about 1236. The pilots proceeded to Daniels Summit Lodge, Heber, Utah, where they arrived about 1300 and remained until about 1450. After departing the lodge, the flight-of-two proceeded to Wolf Creek Summit. The R66 pilot stated he landed first in a large snow-covered area when they arrived at Wolf Creek Summit. According to the 206L-1 pilot, he prepared to land by conducting a power check and determined that the wind was light, and the helicopter had adequate power. The 206L-1 pilot then landed about 100 ft behind the R66. Upon touchdown, the skids teetered aft, so he brought the helicopter to a hover, then increased power to depart. While about 150 ft above ground level and above effective translational lift, the helicopter began to rotate clockwise about its vertical axis despite full application of left anti-torque pedal and lowering the collective. The helicopter impacted trees and descended to the snow-covered terrain. Multiple videos, captured by witnesses near the accident site, recorded the helicopter in the air, rotating about its vertical axis before it impacted trees and descended to the ground. Postaccident examination revealed the helicopter came to rest on its left side on soft snow, surrounded by trees of about 40 to 50 ft in height, at an elevation of about 9,450 ft mean sea level. All major components remained on or near the main wreckage. The tailboom separated from the fuselage. The aft end of the tailboom, that included the tail rotor gearbox and tail rotor assembly, separated from the tailboom. One tail rotor blade was about 50 ft from the main wreckage. The other tail rotor blade was not recovered. At least one main rotor blade fractured into multiple sections, while the other was partially buried in the soft snow. The helicopter was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260119202313.s: The pilot of a Bell 206L-1 helicopter experienced an uncommanded clockwise rotation while hovering 150 feet above ground level at Wolf Creek Summit, Utah, despite applying full left anti-torque pedal. The helicopter subsequently impacted trees and crashed into snow-covered terrain, resulting in substantial damage and minor injuries to the pilot and three passengers.

NTSB:20260120202315.n: Two helicopters were conducting low-altitude wildlife capture operations in mountainous terrain when they collided mid-air. Both helicopters were substantially damaged; the pilots and passenger were uninjured. The pilots and passengers briefed their operational plan prior to departing. The first helicopter (N74730) was assigned to a northern sector and would perform operations starting on the north edge of that sector, working south. The second helicopter (N996NR) was assigned a sector bordering the southern boundary of the north sector and would begin its operations at the southernmost portion of its assigned sector, working north. The pilots each planned to meet at a fuel truck located near the common border of the two sectors. The operational area was in remote terrain that included hills, canyons, and ridges. The mission required the helicopters to operate close to/at ground level and included periodic landings. Approximately one hour after operations began, both helicopters arrived in the same area near the sector boundary, where they continued to independently conduct the low-altitude operations. The pilot of the second helicopter had just dropped off his passenger to complete a wildlife capture and had become airborne again. Both pilots reported they were airborne and descending slightly, when the pilot of the first helicopter saw the other helicopter converging head-on. The pilot of the first helicopter quickly applied full up collective control to attempt to climb above the flight path of the converging helicopter, and as they passed the helicopters collided. The collision resulted in substantial damage to the tail section of the first helicopter. The pilots stated they believed the accident could have been avoided with better radio communication. Additionally, the pilots reported that the terrain’s effect on radio transmissions and the operational workload prevented continuous and unreliable communication between the helicopters; therefore, they relied on see-and-avoid techniques to ensure safe separation. The pilots of both helicopters reported no mechanical malfunctions or anomalies that would have precluded normal operations.
